questions.question: Which of the following is expressly outside the scope of TR84?

options.A: Facilities manufacturing clinical trial materials
options.B: Data integrity management in clinical practice and the conduct of clinical trials
options.C: Packaging and labeling operation data, including in-process controls
options.D: Facilities manufacturing, packaging, or storing APIs and intermediates

questions.explanation: TR84 applies to facilities that manufacture, process, package, or store finished products, APIs, and intermediates, including manufacture of both clinical trial materials and commercial products, and it also covers packaging and labeling and IPC data. It expressly states, however, that it does not apply to DI management in clinical practice and the conduct of clinical trials; laboratory DI is addressed separately in TR80.

questions.question: What industry difficulty does TR84 aim to address, and what approach does it propose?

options.A: Uncertainty about whether production data also needs DI controls; the approach is to apply the highest level of control and review to every manufacturing step
options.B: Electronic systems are too costly; the approach is to return entirely to paper records and add second-person witnessing to reduce risk
options.C: Review staff are insufficient; the approach is to set the review level of each step by product selling price
options.D: It is unclear how much control each step needs; use QRM to decide based on criticality and vulnerability

questions.explanation: Industry knows that data must be accurate and complete, but is unclear how strong the DI controls and review must be at each manufacturing step. TR84 uses QRM to decide whether controls are appropriate based on the criticality and vulnerability of data for its intended use; it also notes that a one-size-fits-all approach may be neither valuable nor feasible. Returning to paper and tiering by selling price are not the document's positions.

questions.question: According to the definition of "Original" in ALCOA+, how should electronic data originally captured in a dynamic state (searchable, queryable, trendable) be retained?

options.A: It should remain available in a dynamic state
options.B: Printing it on paper and signing it makes it an original
options.C: After converting it to a static PDF, the original electronic file can be deleted
options.D: Only the final reported values need to be kept; metadata need not be retained

questions.explanation: Original is the first capture of information, which may be paper (static) or electronic (usually dynamic). Information originally captured in a dynamic state should remain available in that state, so printing or converting to a static file cannot replace the original electronic data; the definition of Complete also requires electronic data to include the relevant metadata.

questions.question: TR84 defines Data Vulnerability as the degree to which data is exposed to DI failure because of inherent weaknesses in which areas?

options.A: Detectability, probability of occurrence, and severity of the data
options.B: Audit frequency, training records, number of deviations, and CAPA
options.C: The process, the data capture technology, human factors, or a combination of these
options.D: SOP versions, validation status, and change control

questions.explanation: Data vulnerability is an indicator of how exposed data is to DI failure through inherent weaknesses in the process, data capture technology, and human factors (or a combination of these); the 9-Box later also assesses from these three aspects (data management, human factors, GMP process). Detectability, probability, and severity are ATRA scoring factors, not this definition.

questions.question: According to the FDA description of True Copy in the glossary, what conditions must an electronic copy meet to serve as a true copy of a paper or electronic record?

options.A: It preserves the original content and meaning, including the required metadata and the static/dynamic nature of the original record
options.B: It is enough that QA signs and dates the copy; whether metadata and the original format are retained does not affect its validity
options.C: It may only be a photocopy or microfilm; an electronic file can never serve as a true copy
options.D: It is enough to keep a screenshot of the final result and note the date of the screenshot

questions.explanation: FDA cites 21 CFR 211.180 (record retention), which allows retention as accurate reproductions such as photocopies or microfilm, and electronic copies are also acceptable, but they must preserve the original content and meaning, including the metadata needed to reconstruct the CGMP activity and the static or dynamic nature of the original record. A signature or a screenshot alone does not preserve this information.

questions.question: TR84 reviewed about 393 FDA warning letters from February 2012 to August 2019. Approximately what proportion contained DI citations, and what proportion of those related to production operations?

options.A: About 25%; of these, about 80% related to production operations, and the rest to laboratories
options.B: About 75%; of these, about 20% related to production operations
options.C: About 53%; of these, about 45% related to production operations
options.D: About 45%; of these, about 53% related to production operations

questions.explanation: Of the 393 letters, 212 contained DI citations (53%); of these, 96 (45%) related to production operations and 116 (55%) to laboratory and quality operations. The statement "about 45%, of which about 53% related to production operations" swaps the two numbers.

questions.question: What system did the "generic drug scandal" of the late 1980s and early 1990s directly lead FDA to establish?

options.A: The 1990 pre-approval inspection program
options.B: The 1978 major revision and expansion of CGMP in 21 CFR Part 211
options.C: The 21 CFR Part 11 regulation on electronic records and electronic signatures, issued in 1997
options.D: The 2018 DI Q&A guidance for industry

questions.explanation: FDA found that many generic drug firms had falsified production and control records, and ANDAs also contained falsified data. In 1990 FDA then established the pre-approval inspection program, under which a facility inspection must pass before approval, a system still in use today. The Part 211 revision (1978) predates the scandal; Part 11 (1997) and the 2018 Q&A came later.

questions.topic: Four themes of production DI citations
questions.question: TR84 groups the DI citations affecting manufacturing in FDA WLs and EU NCRs from 2012 to 2019 into which four major themes?

options.A: Falsified records, deleted data, lost data, delayed or refused provision of records
options.B: Man, machine, material, method
options.C: Access control, audit trail, data backup, data export and reports
options.D: Poor documentation practices, insufficient data review, ineffective oversight, ineffective system control

questions.explanation: Citations affecting manufacturing fall into four themes: poor documentation practices, insufficient data review, ineffective oversight, and ineffective system control. "Falsified records, deleted data..." and "Access control, audit trail..." are individual categories or control items in Table 3.1.3-1, and "Man, machine, material, method" is the 4M fishbone classification; none is one of the four themes.

questions.question: Of the 82 EU NCRs containing DI citations from January 2012 to August 2018, how are the falsification-related issues distributed?

options.A: Production 22%, laboratory 46%, both 32%
options.B: Production 46%, laboratory 22%, both 32%
options.C: Production 32%, laboratory 46%, both 22%
options.D: Production 50%, laboratory 50%, both 0% (no overlap)

questions.explanation: Of 163 NCRs, 82 (50%) contained DI citations; of these 82, about 46% involved falsification in production systems, 22% in laboratory systems, and 32% in both. Falsification in production is thus more common than in laboratories, which is one reason TR84 focuses on manufacturing.

questions.topic: Warning letter example — PLC vs batch record
questions.question: What production DI problem was identified in the July 2019 FDA warning letter cited by TR84?

options.A: The audit trail function of the tablet press PLC was disabled
options.B: Operators deleted HMI data in the batch record
options.C: Data changes in the batch record were written in pencil
options.D: Handwritten batch record values were always within range, yet PLC-recorded values often exceeded it

questions.explanation: That WL noted that the handwritten values in batch records were always within the process parameter range, while the values recorded by the tablet press PLC frequently exceeded the established range. A separate December 2019 WL involved numerous discrepancies between HMI data and what operators entered in the batch record. A disabled audit trail and pencil records are other examples in Table 3.1.3-1, not the content of this letter.

questions.question: According to §4.1, when should a DI risk assessment be performed when introducing a new data management system?

options.A: Proactively at implementation, and brought into that system's change control
options.B: After the system has been live and stable for one year, as a retrospective risk assessment
options.C: Only after an official inspection or internal audit finds a deficiency
options.D: Together with the annual product review (APR)

questions.explanation: Risk assessment should be performed proactively when a new system is introduced and brought into overarching change control, as a preventive measure. It should also be performed for existing systems, after deviations or incidents, and when the system changes. Waiting a year after go-live, waiting for an inspection, or waiting for the APR defeats the preventive purpose.

questions.question: An operator did not pay attention to a mixing operation, let it run beyond the validated time, and then wrote in-range values in the record. According to TR84's human factors classification, which type is this?

options.A: Attention failure: an unintentional action error
options.B: Knowledge gap: a thinking error caused by insufficient training
options.C: Misconduct: intentional behavior, writing false records to cover up a mistake
options.D: Memory failure: an action error of forgetting the sequence of steps

questions.explanation: Not paying attention to the mixing time is itself an oversight, but afterward writing false in-range values is deliberate concealment, and TR84 lists this scenario as misconduct (intentional behavior). Intentional behavior requires a full investigation and may call for forensic techniques; unintentional errors (attention, memory, knowledge, procedure gap) are handled by risk assessment to find where things might go wrong.

questions.question: A process parameter is not a CQA/CPP but must be tightly controlled to ensure process consistency. According to Table 4.2.1-1, what is its data criticality?

options.A: High, because all manufacturing data is critical
options.B: Medium, related to process robustness and consistency
options.C: Low, because it does not affect any CQA
options.D: Not GMP data, so no classification is needed

questions.explanation: Data that directly affects product quality or safety (CQA, CPP) is High; data related to process robustness and consistency, not a CQA/CP/CPP but needing tight control, is Medium; data that is neither and only demonstrates GMP compliance is Low. Although TR84 says all manufacturing data is critical, criticality levels still differ with intended use.

questions.question: An operation falls in the orange box of the 9-Box (H/M: High criticality, Medium control). What is TR84's direction for improvement?

options.A: Reclassify the data as Medium criticality to move it out of orange
options.B: Reduce the review frequency for this operation and move the resources to the red box
options.C: Move up from bottom to top in the grid, raising the data criticality
options.D: Raise the data control level, moving from right to left in the grid

questions.explanation: The goal is to make controls commensurate with data criticality and avoid landing in red or orange; the mitigation strategy is to add controls, moving from right to left. Criticality is determined by the use of the data and cannot be downgraded just to move out of a box. Shifting resources is the situation for the blue box (controls may exceed what is needed), and even then it does not mean reducing controls.

questions.question: In Case 2, total granulation time is written into a QU-approved recipe and controlled by a validated PLC, with automatic alerts on the printed report when outside the validated range. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: The control level is still Low, and each batch still needs peer review and QU review
options.B: The control level is High, no second-person verification is needed, and the QU still reviews the complete BPR
options.C: The control level is High, and the QU need not review the BPR at release either
options.D: The control level is Medium, and supervisor real-time witnessing is needed instead

questions.explanation: Case 1 is entirely manual, relying on second-person verification and QU review, and the control level is Low. Case 2 uses a validated PLC to capture data automatically, not relying on human intervention, so the control level is High; with the PLC report and out-of-limit alert, batch-by-batch second-person verification is no longer needed, but the QU still reviews the complete BPR at release.

questions.question: What is TR84's position on intentional falsification and deliberate manipulation of data?

options.A: It can be tolerated for Low criticality data that falls in the blue box
options.B: Residual falsification risk is acceptable as long as High-level data controls are in place
options.C: It is acceptable as long as it is detected before batch release
options.D: It is unacceptable regardless of criticality, vulnerability, or existing controls

questions.explanation: TR84's risk tiering is used to decide control strength, not to tolerate falsification. §5.0 states that intentional fraud and data manipulation are not acceptable under any circumstances, regardless of data criticality, vulnerability, or the level of existing controls; §4.3 also says the 9-Box leaves no room for falsification.

questions.question: How does §5.0 describe the relationship between regulatory guidance and DI controls?

options.A: Regulatory guidance explains the "how", and DI controls explain the "what" to be achieved
options.B: Regulatory guidance explains the "what", and DI controls are the "how" of implementation
options.C: Both apply only to electronic systems; paper is out of scope
options.D: Regulatory guidance governs the laboratory, and DI controls govern only the production floor

questions.explanation: Documents from WHO, FDA, MHRA, PIC/S, and others explain what is needed to ensure DI (the what); DI controls are how those requirements are put into practice (the how), and can be written into operating procedures or included in computerized system validation and equipment qualification. Controls apply to paper, electronic, and hybrid systems.

questions.question: One person makes a typing error on a sterile filling critical parameter record, and another makes a typing error on a training record. According to §5.1, how do the correction requirements for the two differ?

options.A: The filling record requires QA-witnessed correction, while the training record can be overwritten directly
options.B: The training record is Low criticality, so no reason for the correction need be given
options.C: There is no difference; both require a signature, the time, and the reason, with the original content retained
options.D: The filling record must be voided and rewritten, while the training record may be corrected with a single line

questions.explanation: TR84 uses this example to show that some controls do not differ by criticality: both persons must make the necessary correction, state the reason, sign, and record the time, and the original content must remain legible. Requirements that apply uniformly like this are basic elements of the QMS and are outside the differentiated controls TR84 discusses.

questions.question: According to §5.1–5.2, which of the following sets of control aspects does TR84 consider can be differentiated by criticality?

options.A: Control frequency, who performs it, and how detailed the review is
options.B: Whether an SOP, training, and system validation are required
options.C: Whether electronic signatures require time stamps and permanent links
options.D: Who may change the system date and time

questions.explanation: What can be differentiated is the degree of control, such as frequency (daily or monthly), the performer (manufacturing or QU), and the amount of review detail. SOPs, training, validation, and electronic signature requirements are core regulatory elements and do not vary by criticality; the privilege to change the system date and time should be equally strictly restricted for a granulation or a secondary packaging system.

questions.question: Table 5.2-1 lists 7 control categories that can be differentiated by criticality. Which of the following belongs to hybrid systems?

options.A: Retention and access of completed or archived paper records
options.B: Backup of electronic data
options.C: Manual recording or conversion between paper and electronic formats (including true copies)
options.D: Issuance (generation) and reconciliation of documents

questions.explanation: Of the 7 categories, paper has 2 (retention and access of paper records, and issuance and reconciliation of documents); hybrid has 1 (manual recording or conversion between paper and electronic formats, including true copies); electronic has 4 (access control, audit trail review, backup, and use of electronic data). Requirements that cannot be differentiated are regarded as core QMS elements and are outside the scope of this TR.

questions.question: For systems storing High criticality data (such as an MES, a historian, or a filter integrity tester used for aseptic filling), what credential control does TR84 give as an example?

options.A: Change password every 180 days, lock out after 10 failed attempts, no reuse within 5 generations
options.B: Change password every 90 days, lock out after 5 failed attempts, no reuse within 10 generations
options.C: Change password annually, no lockout, group accounts allowed
options.D: Change password every 90 days, lock out after 10 failed attempts, no reuse within 5 generations

questions.explanation: High: a unique ID and password for each user, password change every 90 days, lockout after 5 failed attempts, reuse only after 10 generations, and annual account review. "Change password every 180 days, lock out after 10 failed attempts" are the Medium numbers; "change password annually, no lockout, group accounts allowed" is the Low practice (for example, a packaging line HMI that stores no data may use a passcode or group account, changed annually, with no lockout). These frequencies are for illustration only, and each company should decide on a risk basis.

questions.question: The charged weight cannot be captured electronically and the balance has no printer connected; this data is High criticality. According to Table 5.3.3.1-1, how should it be verified?

options.A: A peer verifies in real time at the moment of charging (four-eyes), and the QU reviews before release
options.B: A peer checks the record after the fact, before the next critical step or before batch release
options.C: A peer need only perform a general GDP check, without verifying the accuracy of the values
options.D: The operator personally rechecks the values at the end of the batch and signs to confirm

questions.explanation: Where there is no controlled second format (audit trail, printout, photograph, etc.), High criticality data must be verified in real time by a peer that the quantity is correct and the record is accurate (four-eyes), and the QU then reviews within the time frame set by procedure. "A peer checks afterward" is the Medium practice and "only a general GDP check" is the Low practice; operator self-checking does not count as second-person verification.

questions.question: For a filter integrity tester used daily, the audit trail element "recipe change" is scored Detectability 1, Severity 10, Probability 2. According to ATRA, what are the total score and review frequency?

options.A: 0 points; no audit trail review is needed
options.B: 100 points; highest risk, requiring audit trail review for every batch
options.C: 40 points; requiring weekly audit trail review
options.D: 20 points; requiring audit trail review twice a year

questions.explanation: The ATRA total is the product of the three scores: 1×10×2 = 20. When a system is used daily or weekly, 11–20 points corresponds to review twice a year (0–10 points event-based, 40 weekly, 100 every batch). Probability is given as 2 because only an independent administrator can change recipes, not operators.

questions.question: A piece of equipment has memory that can hold only 10 batches of data, and batch 11 automatically overwrites batch 1. If it stores Low criticality data (for example a secondary packaging system that holds no quality data such as expiry date), what is the backup requirement?

options.A: The same as High: it must be backed up before the data is overwritten
options.B: It must be backed up automatically once a day, regardless of generation frequency
options.C: Ensure the data is not overwritten before batch disposition is complete
options.D: Being Low criticality, backup need not be considered at all

questions.explanation: For systems with looped memory, High (such as some filter integrity testers) and Medium (such as an on-site pH meter) data must be backed up before being overwritten; for Low it is enough to ensure the data remains available until batch disposition is complete. In addition, for equipment that can back up automatically, backup is recommended according to how often data is generated; for example, if an MES generates data every day, back it up every day.

questions.question: CPP, calibration records, and EM data are to be transferred periodically from standalone systems to an MES or data historian. What control does TR84 recommend?

options.A: Perform it under change control with a test plan, and confirm complete delivery with a checksum
options.B: This is a periodic routine transfer, so describing the transfer steps in a procedural control is enough
options.C: IT staff visually compare the first few records after transfer to confirm the format and values are correct
options.D: The business unit sets the transfer conditions itself according to a work instruction and performs the data transfer

questions.explanation: Transfer or migration of High and Medium criticality data (including one-time migration on software or hardware upgrades, and periodic transfer to a higher-level system) should be done under change control, with a test plan, and with a checksum or equivalent tool to confirm that all data sent was received. Procedural control alone is enough only for Low transfers such as sending data to a data lake for trend analysis.

questions.question: What challenge does §6.0 say pharmaceutical big data brings, making governance and proactive control necessary?

options.A: There is too little data to support statistical analysis and trending
options.B: Regulations prohibit storing GMP data in the cloud
options.C: Data is accumulating faster than traditional human effort can process
options.D: Electronic data is inherently easier to tamper with than paper

questions.explanation: Manufacturing data is being collected at an ever faster pace, beyond what people can handle with traditional methods, so governance and proactive control of data and information are all the more needed. TR84 does not say that regulations prohibit the cloud; §5.3.7.2 even lists migration to the cloud as an example of data migration.

questions.question: What topics will the PDA big data technical report previewed in §6.0 cover?

options.A: Aseptic filling, lyophilization, and packaging validation
options.B: Microbial identification, EM trending, and alert limits
options.C: Laboratory OOS investigations and chromatography data review
options.D: Data classification, ownership, access management, and change management

questions.explanation: The forthcoming TR will discuss, within a framework for governance and control of manufacturing big data, data classification, data ownership, access management, source data, results and data insights, and change management. The other options are not topics listed in §6.0; laboratory DI is addressed by TR80.

questions.question: According to §6.0, what must an organization establish to use information and technology tools efficiently to achieve its goals?

options.A: Processes, roles, and standards
options.B: A larger-capacity historian
options.C: Moving all data into a data lake
options.D: Manual review of all data record by record by QA

questions.explanation: §6.0 says that processes, roles, and standards must be established in order to use information and technology tools effectively and efficiently. Adding storage or centralizing data alone is not governance; since data volume already exceeds human processing capacity, record-by-record manual review is not feasible either. Together, TR84 and the forthcoming big data TR will cover the management of data and big data.

questions.question: §4.5 says a data process flow map is a GMP requirement in some parts of the world. Which document is its cited reference (ref 29)?

options.A: 21 CFR Part 11: Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures
options.B: EU GMP Annex 11: Computerised Systems
options.C: ICH Q9: Quality Risk Management (2005)
options.D: WHO TRS 996 Annex 5: Guidance on good data and record management practices

questions.explanation: Ref 29 in §4.5 is EU GMP (EudraLex Volume 4) Annex 11 Computerised Systems (2011). 21 CFR Part 11 is ref 13, ICH Q9 is ref 8, and the WHO guidance on data and record management is ref 4.

questions.question: Where does TR84 direct readers for general QRM practice (for example how to perform a risk assessment, develop mitigation strategies, and risk communication)?

options.A: PDA TR80 and the ISPE GAMP Guide
options.B: ICH Q10 and EU GMP Annex 1
options.C: PDA TR13 and the FDA aseptic processing guidance
options.D: The PDA TR54 series and ICH Q9

questions.explanation: §4.0 notes that the PDA TR54 series explains QRM more fully, including how to perform a risk assessment and develop mitigation strategies; general QRM principles and risk communication refer to the TR54 series and ICH Q9 (refs 8, 26). TR80 covers laboratory DI, ICH Q10 is the quality system, and Annex 1 and the FDA aseptic guidance are cited only in the filter example in Appendix I.

questions.question: Example 1b: a High criticality reactor affecting an impurity (CQA) is changed to control by a validated PLC, with the PLC printout attached to the paper BPR, but operators still copy data by hand from the HMI. What is the data vulnerability?

options.A: Moderate (Orange)
options.B: Significant (Red)
options.C: Acceptable (Green)
options.D: Negligible (Blue)

questions.explanation: 1a, fully manual with a paper BPR, pairs High criticality with Low control and is Significant (Red). 1b adds a validated PLC and printout, raising control to Medium, giving Moderate (Orange). Only 1c, which adopts a validated EBR (automatic capture, no deletion, access control, audit trail, automatic archiving), reaches Acceptable (Green). High criticality data cannot land in Blue.

questions.question: LOD from API drying is not a CQA and drying is not a CPP, but LOD affects API flowability and downstream drug product processing. What is the criticality of this data?

options.A: High, because it affects the downstream finished product
options.B: Medium, in the middle row of the 9-Box
options.C: Low, because it has nothing to do with CQAs or CPPs
options.D: It is API-stage data, so no DI assessment is needed

questions.explanation: Although LOD is not a CQA/CPP, it affects flowability and downstream processing, making it data that needs tight control to ensure process consistency, so it is Medium and sits in the middle row of the 9-Box. Low is routine GMP data with no direct or indirect link to CQAs/CPPs, such as the between-batch cleaning within a campaign in Example 3.

questions.question: Example 3a: within the validated campaign length, between-batch cleaning of small-molecule API equipment is performed manually, and operators copy the data into a paper record. What is the data vulnerability?

options.A: Significant (Red), because it is manual throughout
options.B: Moderate (Orange), because there is no audit trail
options.C: Acceptable (Green), Low data paired with Low control
options.D: Negligible (Blue), because the cleaning procedure is validated

questions.explanation: Between-batch residue within a campaign does not affect final API quality, so it is Low criticality. Low data with Low control (second-person witnessing, personnel supervision, release review) is Acceptable (Green). Switching to CIP with a PLC printout (3b) or an EBR (3c) gives Negligible (Blue), meaning more control than needed.

questions.question: According to the Appendix I description of the 9-Box, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Columns represent data criticality and rows represent the control level
options.B: The way to reduce vulnerability is to reassess and downgrade the data criticality
options.C: Moving from left to right in the grid means the data control level is gradually raised
options.D: Rows are criticality and columns are controls; vulnerability is reduced by strengthening controls

questions.explanation: Criticality determines which row the data is in (High at the top, Low at the bottom), and the control level determines the column (computerized control in the first column, hybrid in the second, manual records in the third). Moving left to right means less control. Reducing vulnerability has nothing to do with data criticality; it requires adding controls.

questions.question: Humidity during sifting is recorded by a validated BMS (with audit trail and access control), with the printout attached to the paper record. If humidity is a CPP (the drug absorbs moisture and degrades) versus only affecting flowability and not a CPP, what are the respective vulnerabilities?

options.A: Both are Acceptable (Green)
options.B: CPP is Moderate (Orange); non-CPP is Acceptable (Green)
options.C: CPP is Significant (Red); non-CPP is Moderate (Orange)
options.D: CPP is Acceptable (Green); non-CPP is Negligible (Blue)

questions.explanation: The same BMS plus printout constitutes Medium-level control. When humidity is a CPP it is High criticality (Example 4b) and H/M is Moderate (Orange); when it only affects flowability it is Medium criticality (Example 5b) and M/M is Acceptable (Green). With the same controls, a different data criticality gives a different result.

questions.topic: Filter integrity test — FDA vs EU
questions.question: Which statement about the regulatory position on sterilizing filter integrity testing in §8.3 is correct?

options.A: Both FDA and the EU require only post-use testing, and pre-use testing is never needed
options.B: FDA requires both pre-use and post-use testing, while the EU requires testing only after use
options.C: Both regions only recommend testing, with no expectation of post-use testing
options.D: FDA: pre-use testing may be done and post-use testing should be routine; EU: verify before use and confirm immediately after use

questions.explanation: The FDA aseptic processing guidance says filter integrity testing may be performed before processing and should be performed routinely after use; there is no US regulatory requirement for an identity test before sterilization. EU Annex 1 requires the integrity of the sterilized filter to be verified before use and confirmed immediately after use. TR84 reminds readers to comply with local regulations.

questions.question: According to Examples 7–9, under US regulations, how is the criticality of the various filter test data distinguished?

options.A: All three are High, because all relate to sterility
options.B: Pre-use (post-sterilization) is High, post-use is Medium, identity confirmation is Low
options.C: Post-use is High, pre-use (post-sterilization) is Medium, identity confirmation is Low
options.D: Post-use is Medium, pre-use (post-sterilization) is High, identity confirmation is Medium

questions.explanation: A post-use FIT affects a CQA (sterility) and is the CPP confirming the filter was intact after filling, so it is High (Example 7). The pre-use test after sterilization and before filling is a regulatory recommendation in the US and is Medium (Example 8), and may differ in other regions. The identity verification performed before sterilization to confirm the filter is correctly installed is not a regulatory requirement and is Low (Example 9).

questions.question: Example 7c: post-use FIT is changed to end-to-end automation, with the filter tested in-line, no manual start by an operator, and results automatically transferred to a secure storage module. What is the data vulnerability?

options.A: Negligible (Blue), because there is no human intervention
options.B: Acceptable (Green), with controls commensurate with High data
options.C: Moderate (Orange), because a supervisor still needs to review
options.D: Significant (Red), because it is still a legacy tester

questions.explanation: 7a, a legacy tester with a paper printout, is Significant (Red); 7b, a newer tester with automatic capture, secure storage, and audit trail, is Moderate (Orange); only 7c, with end-to-end automation, is Acceptable (Green). Blue applies only to data that is not High criticality, so High data, however much it is strengthened, reaches only Green.

questions.question: Example 10 uses the 9-Box to assess a tablet packaging process. Which stages were judged to have adequate existing controls?

options.A: Planning, line clearance, IPC testing
options.B: Dispensing, equipment setup, packaging
options.C: Equipment setup, batch reconciliation, IPC
options.D: Planning, dispensing, batch reconciliation

questions.explanation: The controls for planning (Negligible), line clearance (Acceptable), and IPC testing (Acceptable) are adequate; dispensing and equipment setup are Significant, and the packaging operation and batch reconciliation are Moderate, needing mitigation measures.

questions.question: Example 10d: packaging equipment uses a group account, and operators can select any recipe and change set parameters and sensor tolerance ranges, rated Significant. How does TR84 recommend improving this?

options.A: Increase the frequency of QU review of batch records after packaging ends
options.B: Record the set values in a spreadsheet, then have a supervisor sign off
options.C: Give each person a unique account, and set product-specific upper and lower limits that operators cannot change
options.D: Keep the group account but change the password once a year

questions.explanation: For both equipment setup and the packaging operation, stronger access control is recommended, giving each user a unique account, or adding product-specific minimum–maximum limits to sensor tolerance ranges that operators cannot change. After-the-fact review cannot prevent incorrect settings; in the dispensing example a spreadsheet is actually considered a risk (easily modified before printing); and group accounts are suitable only for Low criticality systems.
